name: North Branch Bridge
aka: the first bridge over the North Branch

placement.symbolic_location: Across the North Branch on the Kinzie Street alignment, its west landing near the south-east corner of Kinzie and Canal Streets.

construction.note: Andreas: 'It was formed of stringers.' Cleaver: 'The abutments were built of heavy logs.' Two independent accounts, both describing round or hewn timber rather than framed carpentry, which is what this archetype's 'log' value means.

width_m.note: TEN FEET, from Charles Cleaver, of both branch bridges. This is the only dimension of any structure in this dataset that a source actually states, and it is worth saying why it is trusted at tier 2: Cleaver was recalling a bridge he had used and had driven a team across, and a width is the kind of number a user of a narrow bridge remembers. Recorded as 3.048 m exactly, being the conversion and not a rounding.

clearance_m.note: THE PAGE HAS BEEN FOUND AND THIS TAG IS NOW BEHIND THE EVIDENCE, deliberately and for one slice. Andreas prints at the foot of pp. 631-632 a statement signed by J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble: 'These were both wagon bridges, and were about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice freely.' That is the dossier's figure, from four men who used the thing, with a reason attached — the clearance is the winter road under the deck. The value does not move; the CONFIDENCE does, from inferred to documented, and a confidence float is a mesh input (see generators/mesh_inputs.py), so promoting it here without the re-bake beside it would ship a record that disagrees with the committed GLB. The promotion and the geometry repair land together in the next slice; docs/RESEARCH/north_branch_bridge.md section 6 is the finding and docs/STATUS.md section 23 is the work order. WHAT THE TAG SAID BEFORE, kept because the reasoning was right at the time: the project's crossings dossier, docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 5, gives both branch bridges as 'about 10 ft wide, clearing the water by about 6 ft' and tags the pair as documented. The project's crossings dossier, docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 5, gives both branch bridges as 'about 10 ft wide, clearing the water by about 6 ft' and tags the pair as documented. The width is documented and now has its source; the clearance does not. Searching the transcriptions that carry the rest of this bridge's evidence returns the width, the log abutments, the stringers and the 1832 date, and nothing anywhere about a height above the water. The number is kept because it is the dossier's and because it is plausible for a stringer bridge crossing shallow water with cribbed abutments, but it is recorded as INFERRED until the page behind it is found. See docs/RESEARCH/north_branch_bridge.md. The archetype's DOC_CLEARANCE_M constant carried the same overstatement and its docstring is corrected in the same slice.

abutments.note: 'The abutments were built of heavy logs in the shallow water near the banks.' The one structural statement anybody made about these bridges, and it is specific: the ends were carried on log cribs standing OUT IN THE WATER rather than on dry-land bearings.

pier_kind.note: THIS RECORD PICKED THE DISAGREEMENT AND PICKED IT WRONG, and the source that settles it was signed by the eyewitness this record leaned on. The 1883 old-settlers statement printed at Andreas pp. 631-632 — Caton, Bates, CLEAVER and Noble — says 'both bridges were built on abutments and two "bents"', and describes them: 'The bents were of four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water.' So 'Bent' in the Kinzie Street page's chronology table is not a modern type-word applied down a column, as the reasoning below assumed; it is very probably that table reading this footnote, and it is the settlers' own word. A bent of four heavy logs standing on the channel bottom is not a crib. The value stays 'crib' for exactly one slice, because it is a mesh input and the committed GLB is built from it; the correction lands with the re-bake — see docs/STATUS.md section 23. THE SUPERSEDED REASONING, kept because it is what an honest reading of the thinner evidence looked like: A DISAGREEMENT PICKED WITH REASONING RATHER THAN SILENTLY. Cleaver describes heavy logs standing in shallow water, which is a crib — a log box, sunk and filled. The Kinzie Street page's chronology table instead types the bridge 'Wood, Fixed, Bent', and a bent is framed and usually pile-borne. Crib is adopted because Cleaver is an eyewitness describing what he saw and the table is a modern editorial classification applied uniformly down a column covering six bridges and a century. THE INFERENCE IS THE STEP FROM ABUTMENTS TO PIERS, not the choice between the two words: Cleaver describes the ends, nobody describes the middle, and this record assumes the intermediate supports were built the way the ends were.

pier_spacing_m.note: IT IS ATTESTED NOW, AND THE ANSWER IS TWO. The 1883 old-settlers statement at Andreas pp. 631-632 (source old_settlers_bridges_1883, not cited on this attribute because the shipped value is still the invention) says both branch bridges 'were built on abutments and two "bents"', with 'stringers of heavy logs stretched from the abutments to the bents, and between the bents'. Two intermediate supports, not fifteen; and the archetype's regular 4.5 m colonnade is not the shape of the structure the letter describes, which is a three-span crossing. The number below is what the committed mesh is built from and it is wrong; it stays until the record change and the re-bake land together, because a value a generator reads cannot move here without the geometry moving with it. docs/LIBERTIES.md L29 carries the admission and its 2026-08-10 update; docs/STATUS.md section 23 is the work order. THE ORIGINAL NOTE, which is the reasoning the invention was made under: NOT ATTESTED IN ANY FORM. Nothing reached says how many supports this bridge had, how far apart they stood, or whether it had any at all between its abutments. It must have had some — 71.83 m is far beyond any log stringer — but the number is the archetype's default, retained deliberately rather than replaced by a fresh guess, and it sets the bay count at 16 and therefore puts 15 cribs in the river. That is the most conspicuous invention in this structure: a visitor sees a row of supports marching across the water and nothing in the record says there was a row. Stated on the record instead of left to default silently, which is the lesson docs/LIBERTIES.md L24 was written for, and admitted in L29.

stringer_count.note: THE 1835 READING OF A BRIDGE THAT CHANGED. Andreas describes the 1832 structure as 'formed of stringers and only fitted for foot passengers' and 'useless for teams' even in the summer of 1833; six and a half weeks after this scene's date a procession of hundreds crossed it, and Cleaver remembered driving over it. Something was rebuilt or widened between 1833 and 1835 and no source reached says what. Four stringers under a full-width deck is the later, load-carrying reading, chosen because the scene date is 1835-07-01 and the evidence for 1835 is a crowd on the deck. The alternative — the 1832 walkway, two stringers and a plank — is a defensible model of a different year and would be the right value in an 1833 scene.

railing.note: AN ARGUMENT FROM SILENCE HAS BECOME AN ARGUMENT AGAINST A TIMELINE, and the value survives it. The 1883 old-settlers statement at Andreas pp. 631-632 says the branch bridges were 'about ten feet wide and without railings, for the first few years, after which guards, or railings, were added'. For a scene dated 1835-07-01, three years after the build, 'the first few years' covers the scene date on the most natural reading and the value stays false — but it is now a reading of a stated sequence rather than an absence of evidence, and it is the kind of phrase that will not settle a particular July on its own. If a date for the guards is ever found and it falls before July 1835, this attribute flips. THE ORIGINAL REASONING, unchanged and still the argument for why the absence is stated rather than defaulted: No source reached mentions a railing on either branch bridge; the descriptions that exist run the other way, toward a causeway of logs rather than a piece of engineering. A railed deck reads to a visitor as considered infrastructure and an unrailed one reads as a plank over water, so adding one to look finished would change what the scene says about how developed the town was. The counter-argument is on the record in generators/archetypes/bridge_timber.py: a procession of hundreds crossing an unrailed deck nearly two metres above water is an alarming picture, and that is an argument about the 1835 rebuild rather than evidence about a railing.

function.note: A public crossing, and the town's first bridge of any kind — it replaced the Miller-Clybourn ferry that had run across the same water between Miller's house and the Wolf Point Tavern since 1829. By the scene date it is the link between the West Division's Canal Street frontage and the north bank.

research_note: THE FIRST BRIDGE IN CHICAGO, and the first structure in this dataset that is not a building. It is also the first record here whose dimensions come from evidence rather than from a placeholder: ten feet wide is Charles Cleaver's, and the 71.83 m span is measured off the traced 1834 waterline at the Kinzie Street alignment rather than guessed. THREE DISAGREEMENTS ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN RESOLVED AWAY. The build date: Andreas says summer 1832 and Cleaver says winter 1831-32, and Cleaver was not in Chicago until October 1833, so Andreas is adopted. The capacity: Andreas has it 'only fitted for foot passengers' and 'useless for teams' as late as the summer of 1833, while Cleaver 'remembered driving across the first bridge over the North Branch' and a procession of hundreds crossed it on 18 August 1835 — so it was rebuilt or widened in between and nothing says when or how; the form attributes take the 1835 reading. The pier type: an eyewitness describing heavy logs in shallow water against a modern table's type-word 'Bent'. WHAT THIS RECORD CORRECTS IN THE PROJECT'S OWN RESEARCH: the crossings dossier tags both the width and the six-foot clearance as documented, and only the width could be traced to a source. The clearance is recorded as inferred here and the archetype's docstring is corrected to match. See docs/RESEARCH/north_branch_bridge.md. AND THEN, ON 2026-08-10, THE FOOTNOTE UNDER THAT PROSE WAS READ. Andreas prints at the foot of pp. 631-632 a statement signed by four men who used these bridges — J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble, late in the fall of 1883 — describing how they were built: abutments of logs in the shallow water, TWO BENTS of four heavy logs resting on the bottom in deeper water, stringers from the abutments to the bents and between them, puncheons or split logs for a floor, about ten feet wide, no railings for the first few years, and about six feet above the water so that teams passed under them on the ice. It is source old_settlers_bridges_1883 and it is the only description anybody wrote of how these crossings were put together. FOUR ATTRIBUTES OF THIS RECORD ARE NOW BEHIND THEIR EVIDENCE and are marked so on their own faces: clearance_m (inferred, and documented), pier_kind (crib, and bents), pier_spacing_m (fifteen supports, and two), and the deck, which the archetype supplies and the letter states. They are not corrected in this commit on purpose: every one of them is a mesh input, the committed GLB is built from them, and this project does not land half of a record. The repair and its bake are one slice and it is the next one — docs/STATUS.md section 23 carries the work order, docs/RESEARCH/north_branch_bridge.md section 6 carries the finding.
